task_label: People Task 1 - Develop a common vision
stem: A newly appointed executive directs the team to reprioritize the backlog toward features that generate revenue within the current fiscal year. The approved business case ties funding to a customer-retention benefit, and preliminary analysis indicates the requested features would reduce that benefit. The executive is a named sponsor on the project charter. What should the project manager do first?
option_a: Quantify the effect of the requested reprioritization on the approved benefits and success measures, and confirm which objective governance now treats as primary
option_b: Convene the original sponsors and the new executive to renegotiate the project's success criteria before the reprioritization is analyzed
option_c: Implement the direction as given and record the reduction in retention benefit as a new risk with the executive as risk owner
option_d: Submit the reprioritization through integrated change control, since a change in feature priority alters scope and expected outcomes
correct_answer_text: Quantify the effect of the requested reprioritization on the approved benefits and success measures, and confirm which objective governance now treats as primary
rationale: The executive has authority, but the conflict is between two approved objectives. The project manager must first establish the benefit impact and which objective now governs. Renegotiating criteria, raising a change request, or logging a risk are all premature until that is known.

stem: Three influential stakeholders each sponsor a different outcome for the same project. Available funding supports roughly one and a half of the three. All three outcomes are defensible against the business case. A joint alignment workshop was held last month and ended without agreement. What should the project manager do next?
option_a: Allocate the available funding proportionally across the three outcomes so that each stakeholder receives a partial result, while documenting the assumptions and communicating the decision to affected stakeholders.
option_b: Prepare a value-based prioritization of the three outcomes against the business case and escalate the funding tradeoff to the body authorized to decide it
option_c: Deliver the outcome sponsored by the stakeholder with the greatest formal authority and manage the other two as candidate future phases
option_d: Facilitate a second alignment workshop with an independent facilitator, since stakeholder consensus remains the preferred outcome, and document the agreed actions in the appropriate management plan.
correct_answer_text: Prepare a value-based prioritization of the three outcomes against the business case and escalate the funding tradeoff to the body authorized to decide it
rationale: Facilitation has already been attempted and failed. With the conflict outside the project manager's authority to resolve, the next step is to escalate the tradeoff with a value-based analysis, not to repeat the workshop or dilute funding across all three.
source_references: PMI-PMP-2026-ECO | P5 People Task 5 - Align stakeholder expectations | pp. 7-8

stem: Two senior architects have proposed different technical approaches. Both satisfy the requirements and fit the budget. One increases long-term support complexity; the other increases transition risk at cutover. The disagreement has become personal, the team is taking sides, and the sponsor has asked the project manager to settle it before the next status meeting. What should the project manager do first?
option_a: Escalate both approaches and their tradeoffs to the sponsor, since the disagreement has become personal and neither architect will concede
option_b: Ask the architects to jointly develop a combined approach that mitigates both the support complexity and the transition risk
option_c: Establish and apply agreed decision criteria with the architects and the affected operational stakeholders, and address the interpersonal conflict separately
option_d: Select the approach with the lower operational risk, since long-term supportability protects the benefits in the business case
correct_answer_text: Establish and apply agreed decision criteria with the architects and the affected operational stakeholders, and address the interpersonal conflict separately
rationale: Two viable options require a criteria-based decision, not a compromise design, a unilateral pick, or escalation. The behavioral conflict is a separate problem and should not drive the technical decision path.

task_label: People Task 7 - Help ensure knowledge transfer
stem: A subject matter expert who is the only person able to configure a critical integration will leave the organization in three weeks. Configuration documentation exists and is current, but the expert's troubleshooting judgment has never been captured. A replacement has been requisitioned but not yet identified. Deployment is in ten weeks. What should the project manager do first?
option_a: Raise the departure as an issue and request that the resourcing process be expedited so shadowing can occur
option_b: Extend the deployment date so that the replacement can be identified, onboarded, and able to shadow the expert before the departure
option_c: Ask the expert to spend the remaining three weeks recording detailed walkthroughs of the common troubleshooting scenarios and the judgment behind them
option_d: Identify which knowledge is critical to deployment and to operations, then select transfer mechanisms that do not depend on the replacement arriving first
correct_answer_text: Identify which knowledge is critical to deployment and to operations, then select transfer mechanisms that do not depend on the replacement arriving first
rationale: The replacement may not arrive in time, so transfer cannot be built around that assumption. The project manager must first determine what knowledge is actually at risk. Selecting a mechanism, moving the date, or escalating staffing all precede the analysis that should drive them.

task_label: People Task 8 - Plan and manage communication
stem: Stakeholders receive every scheduled report on time, the PMO confirms the template is applied correctly, and the project manager has verified the reported data is accurate. Stakeholders nonetheless keep asking what is required of them and misstate project status in other forums. What should the project manager do first?
option_a: Identify the decisions each key stakeholder owns and the information those decisions require, then revise the communications approach accordingly
option_b: Compare the communications management plan against the stakeholder engagement matrix to confirm each stakeholder is receiving the artifacts assigned to them
option_c: Add a decisions-required section to the existing report and monitor whether stakeholder questions decline over the next two reporting cycles
option_d: Raise an issue with the PMO that the mandated template does not support stakeholder decision needs and request a template exception
correct_answer_text: Identify the decisions each key stakeholder owns and the information those decisions require, then revise the communications approach accordingly
rationale: Distribution and accuracy are already confirmed, so the failure is in usefulness. The project manager must first understand what decisions the communication is meant to support. Adding a section, re-checking distribution, or contesting the template all act before the need is understood.

task_label: People Task 3 - Lead the project team
stem: An adaptive team has met every sprint commitment for four iterations, but escaped defects have doubled. In one-on-one conversations, several developers say they no longer raise design objections because doing so puts the sprint commitment at risk. The product owner is satisfied with delivery and the retrospectives report no impediments. What should the project manager do first?
option_a: Add a definition-of-done criterion requiring design review sign-off before a story can be accepted, so that design concerns must be raised before work is completed
option_b: Make the defect trend and its link to suppressed design disagreement visible to the team, and facilitate revised working agreements that protect technical dissent
option_c: Reduce the next sprint's committed scope to create capacity for defect remediation and design discussion
option_d: Raise the escaped-defect trend to governance, since delivered work is not meeting quality expectations
correct_answer_text: Make the defect trend and its link to suppressed design disagreement visible to the team, and facilitate revised working agreements that protect technical dissent
rationale: The defects are a symptom of a team norm that punishes dissent, and the retrospective is not surfacing it. Process controls, scope relief, and escalation all treat the symptom while leaving the cause in place.

stem: A regulator with approval authority over the launch raises a concern that the current design may not satisfy a reporting rule. The regulator has not issued a formal finding. The sponsor considers the concern speculative, notes that a formal finding could take months, and directs the team to continue design work while leadership resolves it. What should the project manager do first?
option_a: Continue the design work as the sponsor has directed, and log the regulator's concern in the risk register with the sponsor as the named risk owner
option_b: Ask the regulator to confirm in writing that the concern is not a formal finding, so that the team can continue the design work on a documented basis
option_c: Assess which design work is exposed if the concern is upheld, and take that exposure and the sponsor's direction to the body authorized to accept the risk
option_d: Halt all design work until the regulator issues a formal finding on the reporting rule
correct_answer_text: Assess which design work is exposed if the concern is upheld, and take that exposure and the sponsor's direction to the body authorized to accept the risk
rationale: A credible concern from an approving authority creates exposure the sponsor cannot absorb informally. The project manager quantifies the exposure and puts the acceptance decision where it belongs. Proceeding on a logged risk, seeking a written disclaimer, or halting everything are each disproportionate or evasive.
source_references: PMI-PMP-2026-ECO | P4 People Task 4 - Engage stakeholders | pp. 7-8

stem: Marketing has publicly committed to a launch in six weeks. Operations will not accept handover without a fully trained support model, which requires eight weeks. Finance has refused all overtime. Each commitment was made in a separate meeting with the sponsor, and each group believes its position is already approved. What should the project manager do first?
option_a: Determine which commitment most directly supports the benefits in the business case and plan the project to that commitment
option_b: Present the three commitments and their mutual incompatibility to the sponsor and request a decision on which constraint gives way
option_c: Deliver a reduced launch scope in six weeks that operations can support with existing staff, and defer the remaining scope to a second release
option_d: Convene the three groups to expose the conflict, establish the launch decision criteria and acceptable tradeoffs, and escalate only what they cannot resolve
correct_answer_text: Convene the three groups to expose the conflict, establish the launch decision criteria and acceptable tradeoffs, and escalate only what they cannot resolve
rationale: None of the three groups yet knows the others' positions are incompatible. Alignment on shared tradeoff criteria comes before a solution is proposed, before escalation, and before the project manager selects a winner.

stem: A customer representative approves every sprint review and then relays dissatisfaction to the sponsor afterward. The sponsor has now asked the project manager why accepted increments are being described as unsatisfactory. The product owner believes the representative lacks acceptance authority and is being used politically by another department. What should the project manager do first?
option_a: Establish explicit acceptance criteria and decision rights covering who accepts increments and how dissatisfaction is raised, and confirm them with the representative and the sponsor
option_b: Update the stakeholder register to reflect the representative's actual influence, and raise the planned engagement level so that dissatisfaction surfaces before it reaches the sponsor
option_c: Ask the sponsor to route all customer feedback through the product owner so that a single channel exists
option_d: Invite the sponsor to attend sprint reviews so that acceptance and dissatisfaction are observed in the same forum
correct_answer_text: Establish explicit acceptance criteria and decision rights covering who accepts increments and how dissatisfaction is raised, and confirm them with the representative and the sponsor
rationale: The root problem is that acceptance and feedback rights are undefined, which is what allows approval and dissatisfaction to coexist. Redirecting the channel, adding an observer, or updating the register all leave the ambiguity intact.

stem: A newly formed team is scheduled to begin a safety-critical work package this week. Several members have not yet demonstrated competence in the required control procedures, and an incorrect decision could create regulatory exposure. The team asks to manage the work autonomously. What should the project manager do?
option_a: Seek sponsor approval for a temporary authority matrix that delegates routine decisions to the team
option_b: Use a directive coaching approach with mandatory review gates, then increase delegation as competence is demonstrated
option_c: Conduct a risk workshop, retain the current leadership approach, and monitor the first work package closely
option_d: Assign an experienced mentor and allow the team to self-organize within the existing project controls
correct_answer_text: Use a directive coaching approach with mandatory review gates, then increase delegation as competence is demonstrated
rationale: The team has not demonstrated minimum competence for safety-critical work. The project manager should provide clear direction and mandatory oversight now, then progressively delegate as readiness is demonstrated.

stem: The delivery team maintains an unofficial defect spreadsheet because the formal tool is slow and difficult to use. The spreadsheet contains valid defects missing from leadership reports, and the reporting deadline is tomorrow. What should the project manager do first?
option_a: Reconcile the defect data immediately, identify the workflow barriers, and establish one controlled source for future reporting
option_b: Require immediate use of the formal tool and audit all prior defects before correcting the leadership report

option_b: Request an extension to the permit deadline from the issuing authority, so that the decision can wait until the sponsor returns in two weeks
option_c: Submit the permit application on the current basis and add the community concerns to the issue log for resolution when the sponsor returns

rationale: Analysis is complete and the decision is outside the project manager's authority, so it goes to governance now. The sponsor's absence does not suspend the escalation path, and splitting the commitments or filing regardless both act without authority.

stem: A project combines an AI-assisted triage capability delivered adaptively, a data-center migration with a contractually fixed cutover date, and a sustainability commitment in the business case. Each workstream has a competent plan and a named lead. Two leads have already made scheduling decisions that the third lead learned about only afterward. What should the project manager do first?
option_a: Assign a single lead across all three workstreams so that scheduling decisions are made by one accountable person
option_b: Establish an integrated plan that reconciles cross-workstream dependencies, decision rights, and information flow against the expected business value
option_c: Keep the migration on a predictive baseline and move the other two to adaptive delivery, so each workstream has an approach matched to its uncertainty
option_d: Introduce a weekly cross-workstream coordination meeting and require leads to bring scheduling decisions to it before committing
correct_answer_text: Establish an integrated plan that reconciles cross-workstream dependencies, decision rights, and information flow against the expected business value
rationale: Competent individual plans are not an integrated plan. Dependencies, decision rights, and value must be reconciled first. A coordination meeting is a mechanism without that reconciliation, and reorganizing leadership or approach does not resolve the dependency blindness.

stem: Regulatory reporting requirements are stable and must produce auditable evidence at defined checkpoints. Customer analytics requirements are unstable and require experimentation with real users. Both share one data platform and one team. Governance has asked the project manager to recommend a development approach. What should the project manager recommend?
option_a: A predictive approach with a formally controlled backlog for the analytics work, so a single governance model applies to the shared platform
option_b: An adaptive approach with the compliance evidence produced as a definition-of-done criterion in each iteration, so that experimentation on the analytics work is not constrained
option_c: A hybrid approach, with predictive controls governing the regulatory work and adaptive delivery for the analytics work, defining how the shared platform and team are managed across both
option_d: Deferring the approach decision until the analytics requirements are defined well enough to allow a consistent approach across the project
correct_answer_text: A hybrid approach, with predictive controls governing the regulatory work and adaptive delivery for the analytics work, defining how the shared platform and team are managed across both
rationale: Different certainty and governance needs in one project point to a hybrid approach, and the shared platform and team make the interface between the two the real design question. A single approach forces one side of the work into the wrong model, and deferring leaves the team without a way to start.

stem: An adaptive team can release a narrow workflow in three weeks that removes a manual step for one user group, or a complete integration in eight weeks that serves all groups. The support organization says a partial release will generate confusion and has not budgeted for the additional call volume. Benefits data shows the manual step is the largest single cost driver. What should the project manager do first?
option_a: Evaluate the earlier benefit against user readiness, support capacity, and benefit measurement, and bring the release options and their tradeoffs to the product owner and sponsor for decision
option_b: Release the narrow workflow to a limited pilot group, so that benefits can begin accruing without exposing the support organization to the full additional call volume
option_c: Deliver the complete integration in eight weeks, since the support organization cannot absorb a partial release, while documenting the assumptions and communicating the decision to affected stakeholders.
option_d: Release the narrow workflow in three weeks, since it addresses the largest cost driver and starts benefits realization earlier, then update the affected plans and communicate the rationale to stakeholders.
correct_answer_text: Evaluate the earlier benefit against user readiness, support capacity, and benefit measurement, and bring the release options and their tradeoffs to the product owner and sponsor for decision
rationale: Earlier value and organizational readiness are in genuine tension, and neither the team nor the support organization owns that tradeoff alone. A pilot is a plausible option but is being chosen before the tradeoff is understood or the decision is made by those accountable for it.

stem: A specialist analyst is baselined at 50% allocation. For six weeks, operational escalations have consumed nearly all of the analyst's time. The functional manager has told the analyst that operations comes first. The schedule still assumes 50% and shows no variance, because the analyst has been working evenings to stay on track. What should the project manager do first?
option_a: Reassign the analyst's non-specialist tasks to other team members so the remaining capacity is used only on specialist work
option_b: Establish actual and forecast availability, quantify the schedule and sustainability exposure, and take the conflict to the governance path that can resolve it
option_c: Escalate to the functional manager's superior, since the 50% allocation was formally committed to the project and is not being honoured
option_d: Rebaseline the schedule using the analyst's actual availability, and report the resulting variance and forecast slip to the sponsor
correct_answer_text: Establish actual and forecast availability, quantify the schedule and sustainability exposure, and take the conflict to the governance path that can resolve it
rationale: The schedule looks healthy only because an individual is absorbing the gap, which is neither sustainable nor transparent. The project manager must establish the real position and route the conflict through governance. Rebaselining, redistributing work, or escalating over the functional manager all move before the exposure is quantified.

stem: An external dependency is forecast to slip by four weeks. It feeds two components: one on the critical path and one optional. The other project's manager has not confirmed the forecast and says a recovery plan is being prepared. Your next governance report is in three days. What should the project manager do first?
option_a: Wait for the other project's recovery plan before reporting, so that the governance report reflects a confirmed forecast rather than an unverified slip
option_b: Analyze the dependency against float and release options, develop response alternatives with their impacts, and report the exposure and options in governance
option_c: Escalate to the sponsor now, since another project is creating schedule risk the project cannot control
option_d: Report the full four-week schedule impact in the governance report and request the corresponding change to the committed release date
correct_answer_text: Analyze the dependency against float and release options, develop response alternatives with their impacts, and report the exposure and options in governance
rationale: An unconfirmed forecast is still exposure, and it must be analyzed rather than either passed through as a date change or held back pending certainty. Escalation without analysis gives the sponsor a problem instead of a decision.

stem: Midway through development, the customer says a requirement for near real-time updates means five seconds. The architect designed for sixty seconds, and neither the requirements documentation nor the contract defines the term. Meeting the customer's interpretation may affect the critical path. What should the project manager do first?
option_a: Direct the team to meet the five-second expectation because the customer defines acceptance, then update the requirements documentation
option_b: Continue with the sixty-second design because it reflects the documented technical assumption, and defer clarification until formal validation
option_c: Facilitate clarification of the business need and acceptance criteria, document the agreed requirement, and then assess change impacts
option_d: Submit a change request for the five-second requirement, begin schedule analysis, and ask the customer to confirm acceptance criteria
correct_answer_text: Facilitate clarification of the business need and acceptance criteria, document the agreed requirement, and then assess change impacts
rationale: The requirement is ambiguous. The project manager should first establish a shared, testable interpretation before deciding whether a formal change and schedule response are required.

stem: The product owner prioritizes the backlog by responding to whichever stakeholder escalates most persistently. Benefits data indicates that a quieter customer segment drives most revenue retention. The product owner acknowledges the data but notes that the escalating stakeholder controls funding for the next release. What should the project manager do first?
option_a: Reserve a fixed proportion of each iteration for the high-retention segment, so its features are not crowded out, while documenting the assumptions and communicating the decision to affected stakeholders.
option_b: Accept the current prioritization, since backlog priority is the product owner's accountability and funding is a legitimate input, then update the affected plans and communicate the rationale to stakeholders.
option_c: Present the benefits data to the sponsor and request a decision on whether the funding stakeholder's priorities should override the retention evidence for the coming release
option_d: Facilitate a prioritization session in which the product owner applies explicit value criteria with the benefits data and the funding constraint both visible, and surface any remaining conflict for decision
correct_answer_text: Facilitate a prioritization session in which the product owner applies explicit value criteria with the benefits data and the funding constraint both visible, and surface any remaining conflict for decision
rationale: Funding influence is a real constraint, not something to be argued away, so it belongs inside an explicit prioritization rather than escalated around. A fixed allocation is a workaround, and deferring entirely to the product owner leaves the value evidence unused.

stem: The approved business case commits the organization to a carbon-reduction target, but the target was never carried into the scope or schedule baselines. The team has selected a deployment option that satisfies the baselined schedule and is projected to exceed the carbon commitment by a material margin. The sponsor wants the schedule protected. What should the project manager do first?
option_a: Quantify the carbon variance and its benefit and reputational exposure, then present deployment alternatives with their schedule and cost impacts to the decision makers
option_b: Proceed with the baselined option and record the overage as a lesson learned for future projects
option_c: Escalate to the sponsor as a scope change, since the sustainability target does not appear in any baseline
option_d: Raise a change request to add the carbon-reduction target to the scope baseline, so that the deployment options can then be evaluated against a controlled requirement
correct_answer_text: Quantify the carbon variance and its benefit and reputational exposure, then present deployment alternatives with their schedule and cost impacts to the decision makers
rationale: A business case commitment binds the project whether or not it reached a baseline. The exposure must be quantified and alternatives put in front of the decision makers. Fixing the baseline first is sequencing paperwork ahead of the decision, and proceeding treats an omission as permission.

stem: A team uses generative AI to draft customer communications. Organizational policy requires approved human review before any AI-assisted content is released externally, and no waiver has been granted. The product owner asks to release selected messages now to protect the launch date. What should the project manager do?
option_a: Release only messages above the model confidence threshold and schedule post-release sampling by the approved reviewers
option_b: Hold the affected release, complete the required review, and update stakeholders on any launch impact
option_c: Release a limited sample to low-risk customers under enhanced monitoring while the formal human review continues
option_d: Replace the formal review with an independent business review and document the temporary control for this release

rationale: The approved external-content control applies before release. Risk segmentation, informal substitutions, or model confidence do not replace a mandatory human review.

stem: A roadmap, a sprint backlog, a risk register, and a contract milestone log are each maintained by a different owner. Two of them now report different completion percentages for the same scope, and a stakeholder has quoted the more favorable figure to the customer. The next contract milestone review is in one week. What should the project manager do first?
option_a: Raise an issue and ask the PMO to determine which artifact is authoritative before the milestone review
option_b: Designate the contract milestone log as the single source of truth for all external reporting, and require the other three artifacts to reconcile to it before each review
option_c: Correct the position given to the customer, then define artifact ownership, update cadence, and reconciliation points so a single reconciled view supports reporting
option_d: Consolidate the four artifacts into a single integrated tool so conflicting figures cannot be produced
correct_answer_text: Correct the position given to the customer, then define artifact ownership, update cadence, and reconciliation points so a single reconciled view supports reporting
rationale: An incorrect figure is already with the customer, so correction cannot wait for a structural fix, and the structural fix cannot be skipped once the correction is made. Naming an authoritative artifact or buying a tool addresses neither the immediate exposure nor the ownership gap that produced it.

stem: A sponsor needs a completion date for a board commitment. The team has run two experiments in a new product area and the assumptions are still moving. The sponsor says the board will not accept a range and asks for the project manager's best single date. What should the project manager provide?
option_a: The date the team considers achievable at high confidence, with the remaining uncertainty managed through schedule contingency and reviewed at each stage gate
option_b: The sponsor's preferred date, with a plan to manage scope so that something can be delivered by it
option_c: A statement that no reliable date can be given until discovery is complete, together with a committed date on which the first credible estimate will be available
option_d: A forecast with its assumptions and range, a proposed commitment date drawn from a stated confidence level, and the checkpoints at which the forecast will be refined
correct_answer_text: A forecast with its assumptions and range, a proposed commitment date drawn from a stated confidence level, and the checkpoints at which the forecast will be refined
rationale: The sponsor needs a single number, and the project manager can supply one — provided it is drawn from a stated confidence level and accompanied by the assumptions and refinement points behind it. A bare date, a refusal, or an accommodation of the sponsor's preference each strip away the basis the commitment depends on.

stem: A sponsor wants a firm fixed-price contract for an exploratory design engagement because the budget is capped and cannot be exceeded. Requirements will change materially as the seller learns, and qualified sellers have signalled they will price heavy contingency into any fixed-price bid. What should the project manager recommend?
option_a: A contract strategy that holds the budget cap while accommodating change, such as a phased fixed-price approach with a defined design phase, or incentive terms with a not-to-exceed ceiling
option_b: Deferring the procurement until enough internal design work has been completed to define a stable statement of work, while documenting the assumptions and communicating the decision to affected stakeholders.
option_c: A cost-reimbursable contract, since the scope cannot be defined well enough to price on a fixed basis, while documenting the assumptions and communicating the decision to affected stakeholders.
option_d: A firm fixed-price contract with a detailed statement of work, since the budget cap is a hard constraint and the design risk transfers to the seller, who is best placed to price it
correct_answer_text: A contract strategy that holds the budget cap while accommodating change, such as a phased fixed-price approach with a defined design phase, or incentive terms with a not-to-exceed ceiling
rationale: Fixed price under high uncertainty does not transfer risk, it prices it, and the sellers have said so. Cost-reimbursable abandons the cap the sponsor cannot move. The strategy must satisfy both, which is what phased or incentive structures with a ceiling are for.

stem: An audit finds that all required quality checks were completed and no defects were found, but several checks were performed by technically qualified people who were not authorized in the quality plan. What should the project manager do?
option_a: Repeat every affected check with authorized reviewers immediately, then investigate why the quality plan was bypassed
option_b: Assess the process nonconformance and the product impact, correct the records or checks as required, and address the root cause
option_c: Accept the checks because qualified reviewers performed them, document the deviation, and update the authorization list for future work
option_d: Raise a change request to broaden reviewer authority for this work and close the audit finding once approval is obtained
correct_answer_text: Assess the process nonconformance and the product impact, correct the records or checks as required, and address the root cause
rationale: The project manager must evaluate both process and product impact, correct what is required, and prevent recurrence. Neither retroactive authorization nor automatic repetition alone resolves the nonconformance.

stem: Backlog decisions on an adaptive project have begun altering commitments in a customer contract and a regulatory filing. The product owner argues that routing backlog changes to the steering committee will destroy the team's responsiveness, and notes that no change so far has actually breached a commitment. What should the project manager do first?
option_a: Require legal and compliance to review the backlog before each iteration begins, so that changes affecting commitments are caught before the team commits to them
option_b: Define governance thresholds identifying which backlog changes affect contracted or regulated commitments, escalate those, and leave decisions below the threshold with the product owner
option_c: Accept the product owner's position while no commitment has been breached, and introduce governance review only if a breach becomes likely
option_d: Add the contract and regulatory commitments to the team's definition of done, so that every increment is validated against them before it can be accepted or released
correct_answer_text: Define governance thresholds identifying which backlog changes affect contracted or regulated commitments, escalate those, and leave decisions below the threshold with the product owner
rationale: Governance should protect commitments that exceed team authority without governing everything. Thresholds do that. A definition-of-done criterion cannot authorize a contract change, blanket review destroys responsiveness, and waiting for a breach forfeits the control.

stem: A competitor has released a capability that changes what customers now expect from the product your team is building. The current backlog still supports the approved business case. option_b: Continue with the approved backlog, since the business case remains valid, the sponsor considers the competitor's feature superficial, and the expected value is unchanged
option_c: Assess the effect of the shift on expected value, backlog priority, and strategic alignment, and bring the assessment to the product owner and sponsor for a prioritization decision
option_d: Request that the sponsoring organization revalidate the business case before any backlog change is considered, while documenting the assumptions and communicating the decision to affected stakeholders.
correct_answer_text: Assess the effect of the shift on expected value, backlog priority, and strategic alignment, and bring the assessment to the product owner and sponsor for a prioritization decision
rationale: A market shift is an input to value, not an instruction to react or to hold firm. The project manager assesses the impact and puts it in front of the people who decide priority. Reacting, standing pat, or demanding a business-case revalidation all skip that assessment.

stem: Impact analysis is complete. A cybersecurity control and an accessibility requirement cannot both be satisfied within the approved scope and cost. Both are mandatory under different organizational policies, and each is owned by a different function. What should the project manager do next?
option_a: Defer the decision to detailed design, where a technical solution satisfying both requirements may emerge, while documenting the assumptions and communicating the decision to affected stakeholders.
option_b: Present the documented conflict, the options, and their scope and cost impacts to the governance body with authority over both policies, for decision
option_c: Convene the two functional owners and facilitate agreement on a compromise position that both can accept, while documenting the assumptions and communicating the decision to affected stakeholders.
option_d: Implement the cybersecurity control, since security exposure carries the greater organizational risk, and document the accessibility gap
correct_answer_text: Present the documented conflict, the options, and their scope and cost impacts to the governance body with authority over both policies, for decision
rationale: Neither functional owner can waive the other's mandatory policy, so a facilitated compromise between them has no authority behind it. The tradeoff must be decided by the body that governs both, and deferring to design gambles on a solution that analysis has already ruled out.

stem: A risk that users would reject a redesigned workflow has materialized: pilot adoption is 20% against a 70% target. Release is three weeks away. Analysis shows the workflow does not match how users sequence the task, and training will not close the gap. The product owner proposes releasing on schedule with enhanced support and fixing the workflow in the next release. What should the project manager do next?
option_a: Keep the item in the risk register with increased probability and impact until the release decision is made
option_b: Accept the product owner's proposal, since the release date is committed, enhanced support is available, and a workflow fix is already planned for the next release
option_c: Treat the materialized risk as an issue, and present the intervention options, their release and benefit impacts, and a recommendation to the decision makers
option_d: Delay the release until the workflow has been redesigned around the users' actual task sequence and re-piloted with the affected user group
correct_answer_text: Treat the materialized risk as an issue, and present the intervention options, their release and benefit impacts, and a recommendation to the decision makers
rationale: A materialized risk is an issue, and the release decision now carries a known benefit shortfall that the decision makers have not seen. The product owner cannot absorb that tradeoff alone, a unilateral delay preempts it, and leaving it in the risk register misclassifies what has already happened.

stem: An independent market analysis, accepted by the sponsoring organization, shows the project's remaining benefits no longer justify the remaining investment. Schedule and cost performance are healthy, the team is highly engaged, and roughly 70% of the budget has already been spent. What should the project manager do next?
option_a: Prepare and present a continue, pivot, or terminate recommendation to governance, based on the remaining investment against the revised benefits
option_b: Continue to completion, since most of the investment is already committed and performance remains strong
option_c: Reduce the remaining scope to those elements that still deliver benefit, and complete the project within the reduced scope and the remaining budget
option_d: Rebaseline the project's success measures to reflect the revised market conditions and continue against the new baseline
correct_answer_text: Prepare and present a continue, pivot, or terminate recommendation to governance, based on the remaining investment against the revised benefits
rationale: The decision to continue belongs to governance and turns on the remaining investment, not on the amount already spent or on execution performance. Narrowing scope may well be the right answer, but the project manager cannot select it unilaterally, and rebaselining hides the question rather than answering it.

stem: During a cross-functional iteration review for an enterprise ERP transition, a senior developer points out a structural database flaw that could lead to intermittent data loss during peak loads. The engineering lead abruptly cuts off the developer, stating that the design was already approved by the architecture board and that raising unverified technical objections outside of formal design gates compromises sprint velocity. Following the meeting, the project manager notices that two junior team members deleted their scheduled retrospective discussion points regarding technical debt. What should the project manager do first?
option_a: Meet privately with the engineering lead to reinforce psychological safety, and work with the team to establish clear working agreements that explicitly protect constructive technical dissent
option_b: Add the structural database flaw directly to the product backlog and assign it to the senior developer for mandatory remediation in the next sprint
option_c: Convene an extraordinary session of the architecture board to independently audit the database design and settle the technical disagreement
option_d: Instruct the junior team members to restore their deleted retrospective points to ensure artifact transparency for leadership review
correct_answer_text: Meet privately with the engineering lead to reinforce psychological safety, and work with the team to establish clear working agreements that explicitly protect constructive technical dissent
rationale: The team is exhibiting signs of defensive whispering and fear of reprisal, indicating a collapse in psychological safety. The leader must treat the behavioral and systemic cultural breakdown first. Forcing junior members to type points or bypassing the lead to push technical fixes directly treats symptoms rather than the root cause.

The North American operations lead insists on a centralized, highly controlled data layer to protect stability, while the European engineering lead refuses to proceed unless a decentralized microservices model is used to meet local privacy expectations. What should the project manager do next?

option_b: Direct the team to build a hybrid, dual-layered data model that incorporates both approaches to preserve consensus and restore team velocity
option_c: Settle the dispute by selecting the decentralized model because regulatory privacy factors carry a higher inherent project risk
option_d: Facilitate an emergency evaluation session with both leads using objective criteria tied directly to the business case requirements, and address the interpersonal behavior separately

rationale: When technical conflicts stall delivery, the project manager must separate the logical decision path from the interpersonal behavioral breakdown. stem: A multi-year automated logistics project has consumed 85% of its allocated contingency reserve due to a series of realized risk events, but only 45% of the planned work is complete. A predictive forecast indicates that upcoming integration phases will trigger secondary risks that are highly likely to exceed the remaining approved budget baseline. The project manager needs to secure additional funding to protect project viability. What is the most appropriate financial strategy?
option_a: Formally request a release of funding from the management reserve by presenting a detailed risk realization report, an updated Cost Performance Index (CPI) forecast, and a mitigation roadmap to the governance board
option_b: Unilaterally apply a 15% budget reduction across all remaining project work packages to artificially replenish the spent contingency reserve, while documenting the assumptions and communicating the decision to affected stakeholders.
option_c: Instruct the team to pause work on low-value deliverables and allocate their remaining labor budgets directly into the risk remediation fund, while documenting the assumptions and communicating the decision to affected stakeholders.
option_d: Rebaseline the project's cost metrics immediately to fold the projected overage into a new approved budget baseline without triggering a threshold breach, then monitor the outcome through the next reporting cycle.
correct_answer_text: Formally request a release of funding from the management reserve by presenting a detailed risk realization report, an updated Cost Performance Index (CPI) forecast, and a mitigation roadmap to the governance board
rationale: Contingency reserve is controlled by the project manager for identified risks, but accessing management reserves for unforeseen impacts or systemic overruns requires passing a defined governance threshold. The PM must present transparent, quantitative evidence to the body holding that authority rather than manipulating internal work packages or silently rebaselining.

stem: A complex hospital infrastructure retrofit is running on a highly optimized, tight critical path. During validation testing, a senior medical equipment supplier realizes that an approved operational workflow requires specialized ventilation clearances that were completely omitted from the master architectural blueprints. Implementing the design change right now will consume the remaining project float and slip the opening milestone by three weeks. The customer's clinical director verbally promises to secure a local building department variance after launch if the team maintains the current timeline. What is the correct next step for the project manager?
option_a: Instruct the construction team to execute a fast-track workaround based on the clinical director's verbal guarantee to secure the variance post-launch
option_b: Document the technical scope omission, model the downstream critical path and cost impacts, submit a formal change request to change control, and perform no unauthorized modification to the physical structure
option_c: Halt all construction work packages immediately and request a formal project closure review due to a fatal, non-recoverable architectural scope error
option_d: Unilaterally draw down the project's management reserve to fund overnight shifts, ensuring the ventilation clearances are met without slipping the opening date
correct_answer_text: Document the technical scope omission, model the downstream critical path and cost impacts, submit a formal change request to change control, and perform no unauthorized modification to the physical structure
rationale: Real-world survival instincts tempt project managers to accept verbal client promises or use unauthorized overtime to save the date. PMI rules require absolute baseline control: document the impact, use formal change control, and execute zero unauthorized scope changes. Management reserve cannot be accessed unilaterally by the PM.

stem: An adaptive team is developing a remote patient monitoring platform. A week before the pilot deployment, international regulators pass an updated encryption requirement to protect biometric data streams. The technical lead confirms that rewriting the encryption protocols to meet the new legal standard will wipe out the remaining project contingency reserve, slip the pilot launch by six weeks, and violate a contractually guaranteed marketing milestone. The venture capital sponsor issues a direct order to release the current version as a 'limited clinical preview' while a compliance patch is built. What should the project manager do?
option_a: Process the release as a limited clinical preview to preserve market momentum, and create a high-priority compliance defect ticket for the subsequent sprint cycle
option_b: Refuse the sponsor's directive, freeze the deployment pipeline immediately, and work with legal and compliance to present a formal compliance impact analysis and a revised baseline roadmap to the steering committee
option_c: Submit a baseline change request to the Change Control Board (CCB) to extend the marketing milestone, while allowing the engineering team to continue the current non-compliant pilot pipeline
option_d: Unilaterally draw down from the corporate management reserve to onboard external contractors who can code the encryption patch without changing the pilot launch date
correct_answer_text: Refuse the sponsor's directive, freeze the deployment pipeline immediately, and work with legal and compliance to present a formal compliance impact analysis and a revised baseline roadmap to the steering committee
rationale: When a mandatory regulatory standard changes, compliance becomes a binary release gate. A project manager cannot trade legal accountability for venture capital pressure, marketing milestones, or clever rebranding labels ('clinical preview'). The non-compliant pipeline must be explicitly frozen, and the impact must be routed directly through formal governance pathways.

stem: A critical tier-1 software vendor delivering a custom core ledger module for a global fintech implementation delivers a major component that passes all isolated technical stress metrics. However, integrated regression testing proves that the module introduces subtle system latency that destroys the system transaction velocity outcome outlined in the procurement statement of work (SOW). The vendor's relationship director insists that because the code matches the signed-off design specification document, the delivery is complete. What should the project manager do?
option_a: Accept the deliverable because it satisfies the technical design specification document, and open an internal technical debt item to optimize the code performance locally
option_b: Terminate the vendor agreement immediately for total breach of contract and divert internal resources to rebuild the ledger module from scratch
option_c: Withhold procurement milestone acceptance, document the system latency data against the business outcome criteria in the statement of work, and initiate the formal contract dispute resolution path
option_d: Escalate the technical standoff to the project sponsor and request an emergency budget injection to incentivize the vendor to optimize the module
correct_answer_text: Withhold procurement milestone acceptance, document the system latency data against the business outcome criteria in the statement of work, and initiate the formal contract dispute resolution path
rationale: Passing an isolated technical checklist or design specification document does not equal fitness for use if it systematically violates the business outcomes explicitly written into the procurement statement of work. The project manager must protect the project's value by formally withholding acceptance and triggering the contract's defined dispute/remedy pathways rather than caving to vendor pushback, paying premiums, or bailing out the vendor with internal staff.

option_b: Reject the request outright because an enterprise architecture warning automatically invalidates any local scope authority regardless of cost parameters

option_b: Delay all communication until the investigation is complete, and present the resulting cost and schedule impact at the next governance review.
option_c: Confirm the authorized audience, required decisions, and approved message with legal and the incident authority, then communicate through the controlled channel.
option_d: Notify only the affected employees and omit the issue from governance reporting, while documenting the assumptions and communicating the decision to affected stakeholders.
correct_answer_text: Confirm the authorized audience, required decisions, and approved message with legal and the incident authority, then communicate through the controlled channel.
rationale: Sensitive communication must be timely and decision-focused while respecting legal and governance controls.

A regional division manager demands a highly customized, local tax-compliance automation layout for a global SaaS accounting platform deployment.   • Local Scope Tolerance: Delegated PM authority up to $50,000.

  • Project Baseline: CPI is 1.04; SPI is 1.01.

option_c: Analyze the source of scope growth, reforecast the release, and make the trend and control implications visible.

The project manager's change matrix allows local scope adjustments up to $50,000, and this request is priced at $45,000. However, the enterprise architecture board issues a formal warning that localizing the base code will permanently compromise the core standardization objective of the platform.

  • Local Scope Tolerance: Delegated PM authority up to $50,000.
  • Estimated Modification Cost: $45,000.
  • Project Baseline: CPI is 1.04; SPI is 1.01.
  • Division Signal: The division manager threatens to pull regional funding if the customization is denied.
